item.title: Roy Ayers Ubiquity - Change Up The Groove (Remastered)
item.description: Label: Vampi Soul | Prix: 40,00 € | Style: Funk
item.content:encoded:
Label: Vampi Soul

Prix: 40,00 €

Style: Funk

First released in 1974 during his early Polygram run, Change Up The Groove finds Roy Ayers Ubiquity deep in the pocket between jazz finesse and funk muscle. Ayers' vibraphone work threads through arrangements driven by Bernard Purdie's precision drumming, with strings adding a stealthier warmth about the edges. The set moves from the slick, percussive strut of the title track to the supple swing of 'Sensitize', a cover of Stevie Wonder's 'Don't You Worry 'Bout A Thing', and the cinematic 'Mash Theme'. His version of 'Feel Like Makin' Love' hums with soft electric glow, while 'The Boogie Back' rides a breakbeat that's fed countless hip-hop samples. This 2025 Vampisoul reissue comes on LP, restoring a key chapter in Ayers' shift toward 70s funk.

item.description: Label: Warp | Prix: 45,00 € | Style: Electro
item.content:encoded:
Label: Warp

Style: Electro

Last year, someone set up an online petition calling for Warp to re-release The Other People Place's brilliant Lifestyles Of The Laptop Cafe album on wax. Happily, Warp has responded to the strength of feeling from electronica fans - most of whom bristled at the high online prices for second hand copies - and re-pressed it. Drexciya man James Stinson's 2001 solo set remains a timeless electronic classic; a perfectly pitched and immaculately produced fusion of downtempo electro rhythms, spacey electronics and twinkling synthesizer melodies. In fact, you'll struggle to find a better electro album full stop, making this reissue an essential purchase for anyone not lucky enough to own an original copy.

item.title: Various Artists - Strange Weather: A Different Kettle Of Fish (feat Housey Doingz, The Ron Honey Experience, Space Bunny)
item.description: Label: Sushitech | Prix: 50,00 € | Style: Tech House
item.content:encoded:
Label: Sushitech

Prix: 50,00 €

Style: Tech House

Laurant Webb, Dave Coker, Justin Bailey, and Dave Pine were the key figures behind Strange Weather Studios, which was a creative hub in Southeast London that helped shape the very early sound of tech house in the capital. Collaborating with friends and partners on several projects, they produced a number of influential records that defined the genre including under aliases such as Housey Doingz, 7th Voyage, and Space Bunny. This release on Sushitech, which always does a fine job of offering up the best tech house past and present, pays tribute to the studio and its collaborators with representative tracks carefully selected by Laurant Webb and label head Yossi Amoyal. Restored and remastered from rare DATs and pressed up to no fewer than six sides of vinyl, it's a great look at a significant moment in the evolution of tech house.

item.title: Norman Connors - Mr C (reissue)
item.description: Label: Bewith | Prix: 40,00 € | Style: Funk , Disco Funk
item.content:encoded:
Label: Bewith

Prix: 40,00 €

Style: Funk , Disco Funk

Norman Connors, the Philadelphia-born drummer and producer, may be best known for his jazz credentials, but this 1981 gem is a full-bodied plunge into post-disco boogie and slick street-funk. It opens with the radiant thump of 'She's Gone'-a Beau Williams-fronted burner driven by lush strings, sparkling Rhodes and a fat bassline built for roller rinks and basement parties alike. 'Party Town' brings synth-led bounce and slap-happy horns, while 'Keep Doin' It' floats in with satin groove and a vocal glide as effortless as its hook. Connors' use of drum machines and bright, tropical percussion on tracks like 'Stay With Me' shows a producer fully dialled into the era's shifting dancefloor codes. Side B leans in with the sultry 'Sing A Love Song' and the elevational 'Love's In Your Corner', featuring a show-stopping vocal from Jean Carn. The title cut is pure glide: a jazz-funk instrumental wrapped in understated class. This remastered reissue finds Connors' boogie-funk detour sounding sharper than ever-mature, playful, and deeply groovy.

The agenda-setting Sushitech has a just as influential sub-label, Pariter, which welcomes the one and only tech house instigator, Terry Francis, for a rare and essential reissue. Francis was there at the birth of original tech house with his killer Wiggle parties and fabric residency and now kicks off what will be a limited series that digs into his archives. These first offerings were originally released on Eukahouse 25 years ago, with opener 'Notice Board' bringing a thumping low end and wiggling bassline that is topped with smooth chord work. 'Hello, Acid Dathera' (unreleased retake version) is a busier sound with a tribal edge and restless drums and bass with acid daubs and crisp hi-hats, making it a full body workout.

The title track is of course the well-known, much loved and sparkling jewel in the album's crown but the whole thing is a wonderful affair with Philly soul and orchestral jazz-funk meeting in perfect harmony. The stylish and sophisticated sounds here still sound out of this world and cannot fail to get any dancefloor going.

item.description: Label: Star Creature | Prix: 22,00 € | Style: House , Deep House
item.content:encoded:

We're big fans of US talent Byron The Aquarius here at Juno. He is a magician on the keys and so whatever grooves he lays down, they sparkle with melodic brightness. His latest on Star Creature is a brilliantly mixed back that starts with a pretty gritty and dark cut, 'Atliens To Detroit', full of menace and warehouse filth. Elsewhere, there are signature synth glows on the deep and brilliantly undercooked 'Everlasting' while 'Long Way Home' sucks into that sort of dreamy, widescreen and cosmic deep-jazz-house sounds that Larry Heard perfected aeons ago. 'Jamama' is a nice louche and playful closer with fizzy synth fun.

item.title: Joss Moog & 908 - Prodige EP
item.description: Label: Robsoul | Prix: 14,00 € | Style: House
item.content:encoded:
Label: Robsoul

Prix: 14,00 €

Style: House

Joss Moog returns to Robsoul Recordings with something special - 'Prodige', a collaborative release that captures the spark between seasoned mastery and rising talent.A longstanding label favourite and one of France’s most respected house craftsmen, Moog steps back into the Robsoul spotlight alongside Northern duo 908.  The story runs deeper than a simple link-up, with Moog recognising their potential early on and releasing 908’s debut album 'Rendez-Vous' on his own imprint, Ondule Recordings, marking only their second-ever outing.Since then, he’s mentored, advised, and opened up his studio wisdom to help the duo find their footing in an often complex industry. ‘Prodige' is the sound of that mentorship coming full circle.Across four finely tuned cuts, experience and exuberance collide. Hip-Hop swing, soulful textures, flashes of funk and disco finesse are woven tightly into groove-led frameworks that feel both cultured and club-ready. There’s weight in the drums, warmth in the samples, and a looseness that speaks to creative trust between generations.When a master craftsman joins forces with his protégés, the result is more than the sum of its parts. ‘Prodige’ captures that rare moment where guidance meets raw energy, delivering a release that feels fresh, focused and unmistakably Robsoul.

Tracklist:

  • A1.Prodige
  • A2.Crapules
  • B1.You Don't Stop
  • B2.Dress Code

'Paradox' is subset by the fun-loving 'Ychtm Acid' on the B-side, and while we can't claim to be so clever as to be able to decode this standout track's strange titular acronym, we can vouch for the sickness of its eccentric percussions and atmosphere, a fine case of what we call "mood design".

item.title: Chris Pascoe - Mong Juice / Trippy Breakfast
item.description: Label: Evasive Records | Prix: 20,00 € | Style: UK Tech House Reissue
item.content:encoded:
Label: Evasive Records

Prix: 20,00 €

Style: UK Tech House Reissue

Evasive repress seriesWe rewind to 2004, revisiting a quietly influential moment in the Evasive Records catalogue. Following earlier collaborations with Asad Rizvi and Haris, UK producer Chris Pascoe steps out solo with Mong Juice / Trippy Breakfast— a release that captured his deep, late-night take on tech house at the time. Cut with a strong musical sensibility — Pascoe is a skilled bass guitarist, a fact reflected in the record’s sub bass patterns crafting a rich, rolling low end — Mong Juice delivers a dubby, spacious groove driven by reverb-soaked textures and an old-school bleep techno bassline. On the flip, Trippy Breakfast leans into deeper, more tribal territory, pairing hypnotic rhythms with warm minor-key chords. Mixdown came courtesy of the late great Simon Copleston (Iteration X / Rob & Si) at Online Studios, Croydon where Si put his expert engineering touch to the sound of this record. Originally released in small quantities and favoured by selectors who valued subtlety over spectacle, this EP now returns as part of the Evasive repress series — a reminder of a sound built for long nights, locked grooves and dancefloors that reward patience.

Tracklist:

  • A1. Mong Juice
  • A2. Trippy Breakfast

Daniel Poli returns in Poli-phonic wax style, following up two 2025 remixes from last December of Timeless Banditz' 'House Down' and Mass G/Matt Thomas' 'Power Kill' respectively. Those set the tone for an ongoing collaboration between the longtime London underground rider and the still newly inaugural Slow-Wave label; now 'Sin Chronicities' delivers four killer originals from a preciously raw pioneer's perspective, bringing his irreplaceable frontier experience to new moves in the UK tech sound. Add to that a wicked titular pun too. 'Diji Ri Tak' has to be the trancey closer of choice, its synth flute lead cooing like the quantised waving of a magic wand.

Chicago house newcomer Arsene's 'Jack Shit' is guaranteed to detonate on impact, because its 7" release back in February has already done plenty of damage and got shouts from Luke Solomon, Moodymann and Danny Krivit among more. Now the Chicago upstart finally unleashes the full EP with three other, equally fresh cuts of raw, tracky Windy City house. Crunchy drum machines, hypnotic basslines and that unmistakable Chi-town swing are all present and correct here, with dark undertones but persuasive atmospheres all packed with Arsene's own urgent spark. No weak imitations here - this is a familiar analogue grit with future intent.

Star Creature really is one of our star labels right now. The Chicago outlet's next trick is to welcome back Arsene with a second 12" that centres his analogue house credentials. The NYC via Windy City producer moves beyond the raw punch of earlier cuts while locking into deeper East Coast sensibilities without losing that physical, club-ready clout. Each track is built on rugged drums and elastic basslines, always with a sense of movement. There's a toughness here, but also restraint, with grooves unfolding patiently rather than demanding attention outright. Arsene again shows he is one to keep an eye on.

While their sound has long been rooted in 80s synth-funk and boogie, Star Creature has, from time to time, been known to pay tribute to early Chicago house. The A-side of Parisian producer Serious A's label debut, 'Diagonal Wave', falls into this category. Propelled forwards by a lo-fi, mid-80s style Windy City drum machine rhythm, it sees her reach for undulating synthesiser melodies, TB-303 style bass and chords so deep and drowsy they could have been taken from a Mood Hut release. Over on side B, 'Songo Blu' is a more densely layered and immersive affair that blurs the boundaries between crackling early Chicago deep house, Damn Funk, lo-fi boogie beatmaker Onra and the usual Star Creature sound.

The Funkin' Machine are the latest hot property to come out of Italian city Naples, with the band's line-up including members of such celebrated outfits as Nu Genea and Mystic Jungle. You can hear some echoes of those acts across their debut album, Napoletanite - at least in their use of spacey jazz-funk synths, layered percussion and nods to Balearic boogie - but for the most part it's an insatiably funky, floor-focused affair that draws plenty from space-funk, psych-funk and the groover end of the Afro-cosmic spectrum. It's colourful, vibrant, urgent and hugely entertaining - a future classic whose timeless and colourful sound offers more than mere nostalgia for the late 70s and early 80s.
